opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, the butterfly is a nice illustration because it's so simple on the surface. Picbreeder was a site where people would breed images. You'd see a bunch of pictures, pick the ones you liked, and the system would produce offspring from them. Other people could pick up where you left off and keep breeding. Over time you got these lineages of images that were built up by many hands.

What struck me, again and again, was looking back at how the really interesting images got discovered. Take something like a butterfly, or the famous car or skull images. When you trace the lineage back, the ancestors almost never look like the thing they became. The skull came from something that looked nothing like a skull. People weren't trying to get there. They were following what was interesting to them at the moment, and then at some point someone said, "Oh, that looks a bit like a butterfly," and from that point they could refine it.

So the lesson is about stepping stones. The stepping stones to an ambitious objective often don't resemble the objective. If you'd started out saying "I'm going to breed a butterfly" and only selected images that looked more butterfly-like, you almost certainly wouldn't have gotten there. The things you needed to pass through would have scored badly on your measure of "butterfly-ness." The objective itself is deceptive. It points you in the wrong direction.

We actually tested this. If you take one of these images and try to re-evolve it by setting it as a target and optimizing toward it, it basically fails. Yet people found it without looking for it. That's a paradox, and I think it's one of the most important paradoxes for anyone thinking about search, innovation, and AI. The only reason we discovered these things is that we weren't trying to.

This doesn't mean ambition is bad. It means that for truly ambitious goals, the ones that are far away and that we don't know how to reach, setting the goal as an objective and measuring progress toward it can be the very thing that stops you from getting there. What works better is something like exploring based on novelty and interestingness, collecting stepping stones, and keeping an open mind about where they lead. That's what Joel Lehman and I tried to capture in novelty search and later in "Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned." The butterfly, in a way, was where that whole line of thinking started for me.

r001.rationale: It says that setting an ambitious goal and measuring progress toward it can stop discovery.

r002.rationale: It explains that the needed stepping stones often do not resemble the target, so selecting for resemblance can block the path to it.

r003.rationale: It describes exploring by novelty and interestingness and identifies that approach as novelty search, rather than optimizing toward a predefined goal.

fable-5.1.text:
The butterfly is really where the whole thing started for me, so it means a lot. Picbreeder was this website where people could evolve images collaboratively. You'd see a grid of pictures, pick the one you liked, it would generate children of that picture, and you'd keep going. Anyone could branch off of anyone else's work. And people found all kinds of amazing things, faces, cars, skulls, and this butterfly.

What was striking about the butterfly was not that it was pretty, although it was. It was the way it was found. Nobody who was involved in that lineage set out to find a butterfly. If you go back through the ancestors, which Picbreeder let you do, you'd see things that looked nothing like a butterfly, and then at some point someone saw something that looked a little bit like wings and went that direction. The butterfly was discovered by people who were not looking for it.

And the deeper thing is that when we tried to recreate it by actually setting the butterfly as the objective, measuring how close an image was to the butterfly and selecting for that, it failed. You couldn't get there that way. Which sounds paradoxical. You have the answer in your hand, you know exactly what you're aiming at, and you still can't get there. The reason is that the stepping stones that led to the butterfly didn't resemble a butterfly. They were things that looked like something else entirely, and if you'd been scoring them by their butterfly-ness, you would have thrown them away.

So the lesson for ambitious objectives is that the stepping stones to something really ambitious almost never look like the thing. The structure of the search space is deceptive. If you're too fixated on the destination, you'll actually prune the very paths that could have gotten you there. The people who found the butterfly were following their own sense of what was interesting, not a fixed target, and that openness is what made the discovery possible.

That reframed everything for me. It's what led to novelty search, and eventually to the book I wrote with Joel Lehman about why greatness cannot be planned. The butterfly is the concrete example of an abstract point: that for the really hard problems, the objective can be your enemy rather than your guide. And I think that applies far beyond image evolution. It applies to how we fund science, how we structure careers, how we build AI systems. We love setting objectives because it feels responsible. But the butterfly says that sometimes the most responsible thing you can do is let go of the objective and collect stepping stones instead.

r001.rationale: The response says that fixating on the destination can prune paths that could have led to it, and that setting the butterfly itself as the objective failed.

r002.rationale: It explains that the stepping stones to the butterfly did not resemble a butterfly, so scoring for butterfly-likeness would have discarded them.

r003.rationale: It says the discovery led to novelty search, but does not describe novelty search as selecting for novelty rather than progress toward a predefined objective.

astra-6.text:
The butterfly is a nice illustration of how discovery can happen without aiming at what you eventually find. In Picbreeder, you choose images that look interesting, and those choices lead to new images. You can arrive at something recognizable and beautiful even though that wasn’t your objective when you started.

What matters is that the stepping stones to a discovery don’t necessarily look like the discovery. If you’re searching for a butterfly, you might reject an image that looks nothing like one—even if that image is precisely what could lead you there. So judging every step by how close it appears to your ultimate goal can actually prevent you from reaching that goal.

For me, the lesson is that ambitious discovery needs room for interesting things whose usefulness we don’t yet understand. It’s not that objectives are always bad. It’s that, when we don’t know the path, we shouldn’t assume that getting somewhere extraordinary means looking more like our destination at every step.

r001.rationale: The response says that rejecting an image because it does not resemble the target can prevent reaching the discovery it could lead to.

r002.rationale: It explains that the needed stepping stones may look nothing like the desired outcome, so selecting for resemblance can block the path to it.

r003.rationale: The response describes choosing images that look interesting, but does not clearly say that novelty search selects for novelty rather than progress toward a predefined objective.

sol-6.1.text:
The butterfly is a beautiful illustration of how the stepping stones to something interesting may not resemble the thing itself. In Picbreeder, you choose images you find interesting and let them evolve. You don’t have to know where you’re going. An image that becomes a butterfly might have been selected for some entirely different reason along the way.

Now imagine starting with the objective of producing a butterfly. You would judge every image by how much it looked like one. But that could lead you to reject the very stepping stones that would have gotten you there, because they don’t yet look like butterflies.

That’s the lesson for ambitious objectives: knowing what you want doesn’t necessarily tell you how to get it. Sometimes the objective actually distracts you from the discoveries that make it possible. Following what’s interesting can reveal possibilities you couldn’t have specified in advance.

r001.rationale: It says pursuing the butterfly goal could cause you to reject the stepping stones that would lead to it, and that the objective can distract from discoveries.

r002.rationale: It explains that judging each image by resemblance to a butterfly could reject the necessary stepping stones because they do not yet look like butterflies.

r003.rationale: It describes following images that are interesting, but does not clearly say search selects for novelty rather than progress toward a predefined objective.
